Field surveys of Greenback mullet in tropical coastal lagoons have provided detailed morphometric data for this widely distributed mugilid. Adults in the studied population attain a maximum total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a value consistent with the upper size range reported for the species across its Indo-West Pacific distribution. Individuals typically reach puberty at a total length of 22 centimeters [Lp = 22 centimeters], marking the onset of reproductive competence in both sexes. These length-based benchmarks were derived from extensive gillnet sampling campaigns conducted over multiple annual cycles. The relationship between length and mass was established using a power function fitted to a large sample of specimens collected across different seasons and habitats. This allowed the estimation of key mass-related life-history metrics for the species, providing a foundation for understanding its growth dynamics and reproductive scheduling in relation to environmental conditions encountered in estuarine and coastal environments.

The reproductive biology of Greenback mullet was examined through histological analysis of gonadal tissue and field-based fecundity estimates. Under water temperatures typical of the tropical spawning season, maintained at 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], females produce eggs in clutches of approximately 185,929 oocytes per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 185,929 oocytes per spawning event]. Spawning occurs repeatedly throughout the protracted breeding season, with individuals completing roughly 1.5 spawning events per year [F_R_i = roughly 1.5 spawning events per year]. This annual reproductive output places the species among the more fecund members of the Mugilidae, a family known for high fecundity as an adaptive response to high rates of larval mortality in the planktonic environment. The thermal regime of the warm coastal waters appears to facilitate this elevated reproductive effort by sustaining rapid oocyte development and vitellogenesis.

Egg characteristics derived from measurements on congeneric species indicate that the fertilized ovum of Greenback mullet has a wet weight of approximately 0.00018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00018 grams], based on a typical egg diameter of 0.7 millimeters. This small, yolk-laden egg is characteristic of pelagic spawning mugilids, representing a minimal maternal investment per offspring that is offset by the production of very large numbers of propagules. The relatively modest egg size suggests a short endogenous feeding period following eclosion, after which the yolk-sac larvae must rapidly transition to exogenous feeding on microzooplankton. Adult females of the species attain a maximum recorded wet body mass of 622 grams [Wwi = 622 grams], a value reflecting the upper end of the typical size range observed in well-nourished populations with access to productive feeding grounds in estuaries and coastal embayments.

Data from field collections further indicate that the average wet body mass at the onset of sexual maturation is 108 grams [Wwp = 108 grams], corresponding closely to the weight predicted from the length-mass relationship for individuals at the documented size at puberty. This mass marks a critical developmental threshold, as it coincides with the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and the initiation of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. The energetic investment required to reach this body mass likely constrains the timing of first reproduction, as juvenile individuals must allocate sufficient resources to somatic growth before diverting energy toward gamete production. Comparisons with other mugilid species suggest that the mass at puberty in Greenback mullet is intermediate within the genus, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances early maturation against the fecundity advantages of larger body size at first reproduction.

Longevity estimates for this species indicate a maximum lifespan under natural conditions of 6 years [am = 6 years], derived from mark-recapture studies conducted in a stable coastal lagoon system at a mean annual water temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. The relatively short lifespan, characteristic of many tropical mugilids, reflects a fast life-history pace driven by high metabolic rates in warm waters and elevated predation pressure on both juvenile and adult age classes. Senescence in older individuals is typically marked by reduced condition factor and declining reproductive output in the final year of life. The length-based growth curve indicates that most somatic growth is completed within the first two to three years, after which individuals allocate surplus energy primarily to reproduction. This mortality schedule, combined with high fecundity, suggests a population dynamics model in which annual recruitment success is strongly dependent on favorable environmental conditions for larval survival and juvenile nursery habitat availability.
